name: Radium cosmetics

card.summary: 1930s creams, powders and toothpastes containing radium or thorium that were sold as skin rejuvenators and complexion improvers, most famously the French brand Tho-Radia.
card.note: Historical products, no longer sold; radium-containing products were restricted in France in 1937.

quick.overview:
Radium cosmetics were beauty products of the 1930s that contained small amounts of radium or thorium salts and were marketed on the idea that radioactivity could energise skin cells and restore a youthful complexion. The best-known example was Tho-Radia, a French line of creams, powders, soaps and toothpaste launched in 1932-1933.

The appearance claim was rejuvenation: firmer, fresher, glowing skin. Advertising showed a luminous young woman and used the name of a 'Dr Alfred Curie', who was not related to Pierre and Marie Curie. The brand dropped its radium references after 1937 and the line ended in 1968.
quick.how: The products were applied like ordinary creams and powders, and sold through pharmacies and mass advertising, including radio. This entry is a historical record; radium cosmetics are not available today.
quick.risks: Radium and thorium are radioactive, and other radium products of the era, such as the drink Radithor, were linked to documented deaths. Analysis of a 1932 Tho-Radia sample found a very small radium content of about 0.223 microgram of radium bromide per 100 grams of cream. Regulations introduced in France in 1937 restricted radioactive materials to medical prescription.

lead: Radium cosmetics were a short-lived category of beauty products sold mainly in the 1920s and 1930s that contained radium or thorium and were promoted as skin rejuvenators.[3][4] They belong to a wider early-twentieth-century fashion for radioactive consumer goods, sometimes called radioactive quackery, that followed the discovery of radioactivity in 1896.[4]

The leading example was Tho-Radia, launched in Paris in 1932 by pharmacist Alexis Moussalli with a physician named Alfred Curie, and sold across France from 1933 as a cream, powder, soap and toothpaste range.[3][1] The brand's appearance promise was a rejuvenated, healthier-looking complexion, backed by posters showing a young woman lit from below by rays.[3]
The line was reformulated after 1937 and was sold on until the brand was abandoned in 1968.[3][2]

chain: Cream or powder with radium and thorium salts applied to the face
Marketed as energising skin cells with 'rays'
angle.text: Makers marketed radium creams as a way to revive tired skin and keep a youthful complexion, using the scientific glamour of radioactivity. The claimed effect was entirely commercial; no published trial supported it.

paras: In the early 1910s the pharmacist Alexandre Jaboin proposed 'microcurietherapy', the idea that tiny radium doses could energise living cells, and this opened a market for radium products such as the brands Activa and Radior.[3] In the early 1920s Alexis Moussalli created a cream containing thorium chloride and radium bromide, and partnered with Dr Alfred Curie, who shared a surname with Pierre and Marie Curie but was not related to them; packaging read 'after Dr Alfred Curie's formula'.[3][1]

Tho-Radia was registered as a brand in November 1932, launched in Paris that year and distributed through the French-American company SECOR; illustrations by Tony Burnand pictured a young blonde woman lit by rays and were used into the 1950s.[3][2] Other radioactive products of the period included Radithor, a radium solution drink; Doramad, a thorium toothpaste advertised for 'radioactive brilliance'; and Revigator water pots.[4]

In 1937 new French rules limited radioactive materials to medical prescription. Tho-Radia re-registered its brand in April of that year without mentioning radium or Alfred Curie.[3] The company moved to Vichy during the Second World War and recovered from 1948, adding milk, perfume and lipstick to its range; after Moussalli's death in 1955 it lost market share and was sold to Lafarge laboratories in 1962 and abandoned in 1968.[3]

French historians of pharmacy have published studies of the brand's history, including its trajectory from Institut Pasteur circles to radio advertising, and the question of how the cream was formulated and marketed.[1][2] Wikipedia notes that a 1932 laboratory analysis found a very small radium content in the cream, and records that the industrialist Eben Byers died in 1932 after heavy use of Radithor, a case later analysed in a 1990 JAMA paper.[3][4]
No studies found. Published work on Tho-Radia is historical rather than clinical.

Radium and thorium are radioactive elements. The best-documented harm in this product family is the death of Eben Byers after prolonged drinking of Radithor from 1927 to 1930.[4] Sources describing Tho-Radia itself do not report specific injuries, and the measured radium content of the cream was very low.[3]

timeline.event: Discovery of radioactivity, followed by a fashion for radioactive products.[4]
Tho-Radia brand registered and launched in Paris; Eben Byers dies after Radithor use.[3][4]
French rules restrict radioactive materials to medical prescription; brand drops radium mentions.[3]
